text: The head is the single most important Celtic religious symbol. Sculptural and literary references to it spread across the whole ancient Celtic world. Early scholars spoke of a cult of the head, though the term is now out of fashion. Sculptured heads without torsos, read as severed, appear at many sites. Some date to the earliest proto-Celtic culture of the Urnfield period. Some are inhuman and have three faces. One sculpture joined the head with the phallus into a double image of potency. The sculptured head of a sacred animal also carried the same sanctity. The head was thus not sacred only in human form. It remained the most common Celtic religious symbol for many centuries. Myth carried the theme forward. The head of the Welsh hero Bran the Blessed kept speaking for years after death. So did the heads of the Irish Mac Datho and Conaire Mor, though not so long. When the warrior Donn Bo fell in battle, his head sang at a feast so piercingly that everyone wept. The severed speaking head, neither fully of this world nor of the Otherworld, held oracular power and could foretell the future. Koch's encyclopedia records the sculpture of severed heads at the shrine at Entremont and the fortified settlement at Roquepertuse. Skulls fixed by nails to carved stone marked the sanctuary. Warriors cut off and displayed the heads of the defeated, for the head held personality and essence. Livy wrote that the Boii placed a slain chieftain's head in a temple. Diodorus Siculus wrote of heads strapped to bridles or nailed to houses. Distinguished heads were embalmed in cedar and kept in a box for display. The Irish hero Cuchulainn carried nine heads in one hand and ten in the other. Defeated warriors' brains were mixed with lime into a brain ball that served as a weapon or a trophy. Such a ball killed king Concobar mac Nessa. The Celts tied their reverence for the head to that for water. Skulls and metal heads appear in sacred springs and wells, as in the round pool at the Shannon's source.
objective: Document the head as the central sacred symbol of Celtic religion and myth.
key_results: Record the sculptural and literary evidence for the head cult.
Describe the speaking severed heads and their oracular power.
Note the warrior head-taking, brain balls, and the link to water.
